Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Anonymous Anonymous
General Comment
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
AI-RFI-2025-6657.key_quote: I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business... My unique work... was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation... Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent... This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus... on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition... require transparency... disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
AI-RFI-2025-6657.rationale: The commenter argues that AI training and outputs rely on copyrighted work taken without consent or compensation and urges against new copyright exemptions, plus calls for transparency and labeling—captured as copyright/IP and consumer-harm-related concerns. The submission is from an anonymous individual (no organization affiliation).

General Comment
From:
Dane Ault
Artist
Wichita, KS
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a living and support my
family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

RE Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan

March 15, 2025 
From: 
Troy Reilly Jr. 
Freelance Graphic Designer 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence 
(AI) Action Plan 
I am an average American who owns a small freelance visual design business. I have developed my skills 
over years of trial and error, and worked hard to get to where I am now. I am normally not a very political 
person, but I have strong opinions on the use of generative AI in creative fields. The following comment 
clearly and effectively summarises my thoughts on the matter:  
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The unique works of hundreds 
of thousands of other everyday American creators were taken and fed into these AI systems without 
consent or compensation. They ingest the work of these creators, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our 
clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make 
this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a 
machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be 
theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, 
it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big 
Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of 
computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google 
and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these 
things? 
If you want to protect American innovation, you MUST protect American creators. Do not create new 
copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 

●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, 
so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive 
to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value 
generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to 
disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and 
find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
From:
Tariq Al-Rousan
Artist
Concord, NC
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where

our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial

I am an American who works as an artist and illustrator. I have worked hard for years to develop 
the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent 
living until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people like myself. My 
unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was 
taken and fed into these systems without our consent or compensation. They ingest our work, 
reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out 
of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this current administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we, the American people, do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be 
stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a 
new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to 
have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft or other companies, why bother creating it 
in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology. There are some capabilities of these AI systems that could be 
incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment

From:
Vic DeLeon
Art Director

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an American citizen who works for a mid-sized videogame developer, and a prominent voice in the digital entertainment industry. I
have worked hard for decades to develop the skills and knowledge to build a body of work, and have been lucky enough to make a
decent living and support my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. 
They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
This is illegal.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. 
The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by big tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Start by protecting American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow big tech
to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to big tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair

marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Letter Re AI

From: 
Alexander Wiegel 
CA Attorney, SBN 319813 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who is concerned about the unauthorized use of content to train AI. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent demand to create special 
carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of 
hundreds of thousands of everyday American creators is being taken and fed into these AI 
systems without their consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and 
then sell it back to those Americans’ clients – directly competing with them and unjustly cutting 
them out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
they possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 

 
    First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
    Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Americans’ work has immense economic 
value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big 
Tech. 
 
    Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring 
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI 
generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues. 
 
Sincerely,  
Alexander Wiegel

AI Comment

March 14, 2025 
From: 
Jolene Smith 
Parent 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who is the parent of a young artist. My child is not yet old enough to 
vote, but with incredible talent and a drive to be a visual artist as a career.  
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses that exist today, as well as to make my child's 
dream of a career in art and design impossible with their recent demand to create special carve 
outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My minor child's 
unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was 
taken and fed into these AI systems without their consent or any compensation. They ingest 
their work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to their clients – directly competing with us and 
cutting them out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. This work has immense economic value, 
so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them 
to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

General Comment
Hi,
I am a writer with several publications. These works are cornerstones of my career that I’ve worked hard for years to develop and
transform into a profession that supports myself and my loved ones.
Unfortunately, the AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten the livelihoods of thousands of
Americans like me with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their

training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to 
build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, 
so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring 
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI 
generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

among all humanity present and future. A dividend of ALL profits stemming from AI should be distributed evenly. There should be no

I am additionally concerned about biases inherent in the data on which AI is trained and its propensity to generate false answers. We need
safeguards in order to ensure we move towards a more true, just and rational understanding of the world.

What processes do humans need to engage in to build the kinds of expertise that allow them to critically and creatively assess the output
of AI?

something we can reasonably stop. Thus we need to ensure we have a process for assessing harms (e.g., biased output that leads to
increased surveillance of someone,lessens their likelihood to be selected for a job). It is important to recognize that AI is built on the backs
of everyone who has every spoken, written or created anything in any language or form and thus any benefits or profits should be
distributed evenly and fairly. I am ambivalent about whether AI will be beneficial to society, but I am sure it will not be if we don't actively
work to make it free, fair and for our collective benefit not private gain.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: David Soules 
General Comment
This document is approved for public dissemination. The document contains no business-proprietary or confidential information.
Document contents may be reused by the government in developing the AI Action Plan and associated documents without attribution.
Artificial Intelligence, as currently conceived, is diametrically opposed to human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national
security. The US would be best served by cutting its losses in investment in this wasteful and grotesquely overhyped technology.
AI companies have made extravagant promises—indeed, the same promises, renewed every few months when a new version is released,
promising that the new model will succeed where the previous models failed. Training future versions requires exponentially more power
and data for inputs—power which is taxing our electrical generation capabilities and data which does not exist, as we are already training
current models with at least a quarter of the available Internet and thus cannot provide another order of magnitude increase in data that
would be required for linear growth of model capabilities.
Moreover, this training regime requires giving a completely unwarranted exception to copyright law for particular privileged companies—
the exact opposite of a fair and competitive market of ideas. As Sam Altman has stated, AI training is not possible without appropriating
the intellectual property of copyright holders—behavior that we have justly condemned when it has been contemplated by a strategic
adversary.
Despite these very real costs to our resources and legal rights, AI is extremely unlikely to achieve any meaningful progress toward general
intelligence. It can produce an impressive simulacrum of coherent language, but it does not engage in meaningful reflection (despite the
countless metaphors inappropriately employed by practitioners) and its hallucination problems make it unfit to purpose for most meaningful
tasks.
This lack of promise can be seen in the dearth of organizations which have seen significant profitable application of the technology. While
we promise businesses the ability (very soon!) to replace human workers with an automaton, what we have received is inaccurate
summaries, an inability to cite sources properly, continuous (at times libelous) confabulation, and bots that undermine the interests of their
users, making promises contrary to company policy or material reality.
Our country’s interests are best served by stopping investment into this field and instead targeting it to field- and problem-specific machine
learning methods, which do show considerable effectiveness; or putting these resources towards general research and university
education.
Thank you for your attention to this matter.

From:
Matthew Jordan
System Administrator
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to 
build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
●

EthanYu_LetteraboutAIActionPlan

From:
Ethan Yu
Digital Artist and Animator
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to 
build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI Action Plan
AI is deeply wasteful, expending truly ridiculous amounts of energy to shuffle training data around to create the facsimile of intelligence.

livelihoods. Not only can AI not acquire the lived experience of humans, something that makes humans flexible and able to respond in
sensible ways to novel situations, but even if it could we have humans who already have that experience now.

learns patterns in data and replicates those patterns. It learns what words follow other words, and uses those to make reasonable-
sounding replies that can range from deeply wrong to dangerous to simply nonsensical in context. AI should never be used for decision
making, and should really never be used for anything without close human oversight. 
The regulations that were in place were a good start, but they should really be even stronger: ensuring companies that want to train AI
models use only data that they acquire ethically and with consent of the creators, limiting their maximum energy usage, etc. 
The results of deregulating AI would be bleak for Americans and America.

This document may not be used to train any AI models.

Sketch Johnson

Changes to Copyright law for AI

March 15, 2025 
From: 
Tyler Crook 
Writer / Artist 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small business writing and illustrating comic books. I 
have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have 
been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 

• 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
• 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
• 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Name: Anonymous Anonymous
General Comment
See attached file(s)
Attachments
Untitled document

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 

●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Request for Information of AI Action Plan Response

March 15, 2025 
 
 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
 
I am an everyday American who works in the audio engineering business which serves clients 
in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge 
to build a business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently. 
 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses I work with as their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law develops. 
 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology. AI systems can be useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice 
the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting 
copyright law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

March 14, 2025 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give 
effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI 
systems. 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so 
that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has 
immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to 
the original creators, not just Big Tech. 

​
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech 
companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, 
and label what content is AI generated. 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Keith Stanley  Email: 
General Comment
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
We should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until

loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.

should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Julian Plum
Address:
 
General Comment
Julian Plum
Illustrator
Newfield, NY
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small illustration business which serves clients in the publishing industry. I have worked hard for
years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my
family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
